presentingComplaint: Central chest pressure for 5 hours, then progressive breathlessness, sweating and collapse.
history: Ex-smoker with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and known coronary artery disease (PCI to RCA 4 years ago). Woke with crushing retrosternal pressure radiating to the left arm; over the next few hours became increasingly breathless and clammy. Family noted he was drowsy and 'not making sense'. In the 2 days before, he had a productive cough and one febrile episode, and he vomited once with a witnessed choking spell during the ambulance transfer, so the referring team queried aspiration and raised the possibility of septic shock. No melena, no recent travel, no leg swelling or immobilisation.
examination: Cold, mottled peripheries with delayed capillary refill (>4 s). Anxious, drowsy (GCS 14). JVP elevated to the angle of the jaw. Bilateral fine basal crepitations to mid-zones with a soft S3 gallop; no new murmur, no pericardial rub. Chest otherwise clear with no focal bronchial breathing. Abdomen soft, no organomegaly. Feeble peripheral pulses, no radio-radial or radio-femoral delay.
imaging: Bedside echo: severely impaired LV systolic function (visual EF ~25%) with akinetic anterior wall and septum; no pericardial effusion, normal RV size, IVC dilated and non-collapsing. Portable CXR: bilateral perihilar alveolar shadowing consistent with pulmonary oedema, no lobar consolidation. Coronary angiography: acute occlusion of proximal LAD.
microbiology: Blood cultures sent; no growth. Sputum not obtained. Procalcitonin 0.3 ng/mL (low).
differentialDiagnoses: Cardiogenic shock complicating acute anterior STEMI (LAD occlusion, EF ~25%, raised JVP, pulmonary oedema, low ScvO2)

Septic shock from aspiration pneumonia (raised by fever, cough, leucocytosis, witnessed aspiration) - argued against by low procalcitonin, clear CXR fields, cold vasoconstricted shock and severe LV dysfunction
Cardiac tamponade - excluded by echo (no effusion)
Hypovolaemic shock - argued against by raised JVP and dilated IVC
Massive pulmonary embolism - argued against by normal RV and clear LAD/anterior wall infarct picture
finalDiagnosis: Cardiogenic shock (SCAI stage C-D) due to acute anterior STEMI from proximal LAD occlusion
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Cardiogenic Shock and Pulmonary Edema
SCAI Clinical Expert Consensus - SCAI Shock Classification 2022
stewardship: Non-infective diagnosis: the febrile, coughing, leucocytosis picture prompted a septic-shock differential, but low procalcitonin, clear CXR lung fields, a vasoconstricted (cold) shock phenotype, low ScvO2 and echo-proven severe LV dysfunction confirm a cardiac cause. No empiric antibiotics are indicated for cardiogenic shock itself; reassess only if cultures/imaging later confirm true infection. Management is emergency revascularisation (primary PCI to LAD), cautious inotrope/vasopressor support (e.g., norepinephrine +/- dobutamine), and consideration of mechanical circulatory support.
contraindications: Avoid beta-blockers and negative inotropes in acute shock
Avoid aggressive fluid boluses given raised JVP and pulmonary oedema
Avoid nephrotoxic contrast overload where possible given AKI, but do not delay life-saving PCI
edgeCases: Concurrent fever/leucocytosis can be a stress/inflammatory response to infarction and must not trigger reflex antibiotics
Mechanical complications (VSD, papillary muscle rupture) must be excluded when shock is out of proportion to LV function
Right-ventricular infarction can mimic tamponade/hypovolaemia and alters fluid strategy
expectedMaiK: Recognise pump-failure (cardiogenic) shock from acute STEMI despite an overlapping infective-appearing presentation, and prioritise emergency revascularisation and haemodynamic support over antibiotics.
expectedNextQuestions: Time of symptom onset and duration of chest pain?
Is there a new murmur or signs of a mechanical complication?
What is the ScvO2 / lactate trend and urine output?
Any contraindication to urgent PCI or anticoagulation?
expectedInvestigations: Arterial blood gas and renal function
